analysis.one_liner: Bars employers from paying older workers less in pensions and benefits.
analysis.headline: The House committee reported the bill on August 3, 1990, and it was placed on the House calendar, but it never received a floor vote before the 101st Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: In June 1989 the Supreme Court ruled, in Public Employees Retirement System of Ohio v. Betts, that the Age Discrimination in Employment Act did not cover employee benefit plans. This bill responded by writing into the law that employers may not give older workers smaller pension or benefit payments than younger workers, unless a real cost difference justifies it. It would also have shifted the burden of proof onto employers in age-discrimination cases and limited the waivers employers can demand from older workers who give up their legal claims.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers covered by the age-discrimination law — generally people 40 and older — who would gain a clear guarantee that their pension, health, and other benefits cannot be cut merely because of their age, unless the employer proves the reduction reflects significant cost considerations. It also protects workers who sign severance or settlement agreements, by requiring that waivers of age-discrimination rights be knowing and voluntary, and by letting them still file charges and cooperate with the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission.

how_it_helps.text: Declares that the phrase 'compensation, terms, conditions, or privileges of employment' in the Age Discrimination in Employment Act includes all employee benefits, even those provided under a bona fide benefit plan, and requires the amount actually paid or incurred for an older worker to be no less than for a younger worker.
Places the burden of proving that an age-based action is lawful on the employer, employment agency, or labor organization in any civil enforcement case.

Prohibits an individual from waiving rights under the Act except in a knowing and voluntary settlement of a bona fide claim, and bars settlements from blocking EEOC enforcement or a worker's right to file charges and cooperate with investigations.
Applies the protections to all age-discrimination cases brought after June 23, 1989 — the day of the Supreme Court's Betts decision — and to cases pending on that date.

analysis.who_pays: Employers, employment agencies, and labor organizations that sponsor benefit plans would bear the cost of equalizing benefit spending for older workers, or of proving that age-based reductions are justified by significant cost considerations. Plans adopted before the law would have to come into compliance regardless of their adoption date, and employers would face liability in cases already filed.

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs fall on employers, who would have to spend at least as much per older worker as per younger worker for each benefit or benefit package, an obligation that applies even to plans and seniority systems adopted before the law.

The bill would apply retroactively to every age-discrimination case filed after June 23, 1989 and to cases pending on that date, exposing employers to liability under a rule that changed after they had arranged their plans.

The committee's amended version carved out exceptions that weakened the protection: certain permanent features of defined benefit pension plans and certain forms of benefit coordination were exempted, and the Act would not apply to some collective bargaining agreements until the agreement ended or June 1, 1992.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's core promise is real: without it, the Supreme Court's Betts ruling left employers free to pay older workers less for the same benefits, which hits the people who most depend on pensions and retiree health coverage. The honest cost is that employers either absorb the equal-cost requirement or restructure plans, and the retroactive application adds legal exposure. The committee version also diluted the protection with carve-outs for some pension practices and union contracts, so even its supporters would concede the final product was less than a clean equal-benefit rule.

outcome.mechanism: The committee passed it out in August 1990 and it was placed on the House calendar, but no floor vote ever came, and the bill died when the 101st Congress ended.

narrative.text: Congress wrote into the bill itself its finding that the Supreme Court's June 1989 decision in Public Employees Retirement System of Ohio v. Betts made legislative action necessary to restore the original intent of the Age Discrimination in Employment Act: prohibiting discrimination against older workers in all employee benefits except where age-based reductions are justified by significant cost considerations.
Rep. Edward Roybal of California introduced the bill on August 4, 1989, and it was referred to the House Committee on Education and Labor, then to two subcommittees.
The bill drew 117 cosponsors — 106 of 257 House Democrats and 11 of 175 House Republicans — and the Justice Department submitted an executive comment in January 1990.

The subcommittees were discharged on March 28, 1990, the full committee marked the bill up, ordered it reported amended on April 4, and reported it amended on August 3, 1990, as H. Rept. 101-664, placing it on the Union Calendar, Calendar No. 408.

The reported version had been broadened and softened: it allowed bona fide voluntary early retirement incentive plans, exempted certain permanent defined-benefit pension practices and certain benefit coordination arrangements, and delayed application to some collective bargaining agreements until termination or June 1, 1992.
No further action appears in the record; the bill sat on the Union Calendar until the Congress ended on January 3, 1991, without a House floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers and benefit plan sponsors were better off, because they went the rest of the Congress without the equal-benefit mandate, the shifted burden of proof, and the retroactive liability this bill would have imposed. Older workers did not receive the benefit protections this bill promised from this vehicle.

for.name: Rep. Edward Roybal
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on August 4, 1989 to restore age-discrimination protections for employee benefits after the Betts decision.

for.name: Augustus Hawkins
for.role: Chair, House Committee on Education and Labor
for.what_they_did: His committee marked up the bill, ordered it reported amended, and reported it to the House on August 3, 1990.

against.name: House leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a floor vote after it was reported and placed on the Union Calendar on August 3, 1990; the record shows no further action before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was sponsored and championed by House Democrats but also drew 11 Republican cosponsors out of 175, and it cleared the Democratic-led committee without any recorded floor fight.

industries.industry: Employers with pension and employee benefit plans
industries.note: The bill requires the amount actually paid or incurred on behalf of an older worker to be no less than for a younger worker for each benefit, so plan sponsors would lose the ability to trim benefits for their most senior workers. Older workers' pensions and retiree benefits are exactly what employers would otherwise be able to cut, so the industry's interest in this bill ran against the workers it employs.

The bill would have subjected pension plans to the equal-benefit rule regardless of when they were adopted, but the committee's amended version exempted certain benefit practices that are permanent features of a defined benefit pension plan, a carve-out that preserved part of the old arrangement.

industries.industry: Unionized employers and collective bargaining parties
industries.note: The reported bill delayed application to certain collective bargaining agreements until the agreement terminated or June 1, 1992, letting existing contracts stand briefly while union-covered workers waited for the protections.
